common_name: John Baldwin Boxwood (Blue-Tinted Conical Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; John Baldwin holds a true broad-conical habit with minimal pruning, offered by Saunders Brothers as an alternative to Green Mountain.

directions: John Baldwin is a littleleaf boxwood selected for a naturally broad, conical form that needs little corrective pruning to keep a formal cone shape, making it a lower-maintenance substitute for sheared Green Mountain boxwood. New growth emerges with a distinctive blue tint that fades to blue-green as leaves mature, giving the plant a slightly cooler cast than typical glossy-green boxwood. As a Buxus microphylla selection it shows notably better tolerance of boxwood blight than English boxwood, though it remains somewhat susceptible to boxwood leafminer. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and avoid soggy sites, since boxwood roots are prone to Phytophthora root rot.

common_name: Jim Stauffer Boxwood (Jim's True Spreader, Cold-Hardy Globe Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jim Stauffer forms a naturally globe-shaped mound and is valued for landscape durability in colder climates.

directions: Also sold as Jim's True Spreader, this littleleaf boxwood forms a dense, naturally globe-shaped mound of small, glossy dark green leaves, reaching roughly 4 feet tall and wide over about fifteen years. It is little-known commercially but stands out for excellent cold hardiness and general landscape durability, making it one of the better boxwood choices for the colder end of the boxwood range. It shows somewhat better resistance to boxwood leafminer and somewhat better tolerance of boxwood blight than many English boxwood selections. Use it for formal hedges, foundation plantings, or topiary, and plant in moist, well-drained soil since boxwood roots are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet sites.

common_name: Midiron Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy Transition-Zone Hybrid Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs, plugs, or sod once soil is reliably above 65°F; Midiron is one of the most cold-hardy hybrid bermudagrasses available, extending reliable bermudagrass turf into the transition zone.

directions: Released by the Kansas Agricultural Experiment Station in 1969, Midiron is a presumed hybrid of cold-tolerant common bermudagrass and African bermudagrass selected specifically for outstanding winter hardiness. It tolerates winters as far north as Maryland and the transition zone, where standard bermudagrass cultivars routinely suffer winterkill, and it shows notably good resistance to spring dead spot disease compared with many other bermudagrass selections. Its medium texture and few seed heads suit it to home lawns, fairways, and roughs where cold survival matters more than the finest possible texture. Establish only vegetatively by sprigs, plugs, or sod in full sun, and mow regularly to control thatch buildup from its vigorous stolon and rhizome growth.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

common_name: Vamont Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy Appalachian Region Turf and Pasture Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs, plugs, or sod once soil is reliably above 65°F; Vamont is a vegetatively propagated common bermudagrass selection bred for cold hardiness in the Appalachian region.

directions: Vamont is a vegetatively propagated common bermudagrass cultivar selected for cold tolerance and adapted to the Appalachian region for both turf and pasture use, pushing bermudagrass adaptation further north and into cooler upland sites than many earlier selections could tolerate. Its texture is coarser than fine modern hybrids like Tifway or Celebration, but its winter survival made it an important cultivar in cold-hardy bermudagrass breeding, where it was later used as a parent line in subsequent hybrid development. Establish only from sprigs, plugs, or sod in full sun, since Vamont produces little viable seed suitable for lawn establishment. Mow regularly and dethatch periodically, as with other bermudagrass, to keep the sod dense and free of excess thatch.

common_name: Cody Buffalograss (Dense Dark-Green Seeded Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after the last frost; Cody was developed by the University of Nebraska and the Native Turf Group as the first seeded buffalograss with markedly improved density and color over older seeded types.

directions: Cody is a seeded turf-type buffalograss developed by the University of Nebraska and the Native Turf Group as the first improved seeded selection available, offering faster establishment, higher density, and a darker green color than the older seeded standard, Texoka. Compared with vegetative cultivars it is easier and cheaper to establish since it is grown from seed rather than plugs or sod, while still offering excellent winter hardiness and very low water requirements once established. Trials across Nebraska and Arizona show persistent medium-to-dark green color and good summer and winter hardiness across a wide range of climates. Direct sow into warm soil after the last frost, keep consistently moist until germination, and mow high and infrequently for a relaxed, low-input lawn.

planting.note: Establish from plugs, sprigs, or sod (not seed) once soil is reliably above 70°F; Prairie is a vegetative buffalograss cultivar valued for dense stolon spread and good turf quality.

directions: Prairie is a vegetatively propagated buffalograss cultivar that spreads by stolons rather than seed, forming a dense, low-growing turf once established from plugs, sprigs, or sod. Like other buffalograss selections it is exceptionally drought tolerant, needing little supplemental irrigation once mature, and it goes dormant and straw-colored in winter, greening up again as temperatures warm in late spring. Being a vegetative type rather than a seeded cultivar, it establishes more uniformly than seed-grown buffalograss stands, though initial planting cost is higher since it cannot simply be broadcast. Mow at 3 to 5 inches infrequently for a low-input lawn, and avoid overwatering or high nitrogen inputs, both of which favor weed encroachment over buffalograss's naturally tight sod.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

common_name: UC Verde Buffalograss (California-Bred Ultra-Low-Water Vegetative Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Install as plugs only, spaced about 12 inches apart, once soil is reliably above 70°F; UC Verde was bred by the University of California specifically for California and low desert Southwest climates and needs consistent moisture through establishment.

directions: UC Verde is a University of California introduction, developed through years of research at UC Davis and UC Riverside specifically for the climate of California and the low desert Southwest, including Phoenix. It is exceptionally water-thrifty, reported to get by on around 12 inches of supplemental water per year, a savings of roughly 75 percent compared with tall fescue lawns and 30 to 40 percent compared with bermudagrass, zoysia, or St. Augustine grass. Its slow growth means mowing only every two to three weeks for a groomed 2 to 3 inch lawn, or as little as once a year if left as a 6 to 8 inch meadow, and it produces very little pollen. Establish only from plugs, since it is a sterile vegetative selection, and irrigate consistently until the plugs knit together into a full stand.
sources: UC Davis California Center for Urban Horticulture
University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Radar Chewings Fescue (Dark Green Shade-Tolerant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4–5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil; Radar is a Mountain View Seed Research release bred to retain density and dark green color under reduced fertility.

directions: Radar is a Chewings fescue turf cultivar bred to combine strong density retention and dark green color under both normal and reduced fertility inputs, and it is noted as one of the darkest green fine fescue cultivars available. It shows excellent drought tolerance along with good resistance to red thread and pink patch, and it is typically sold endophyte-enhanced for added natural insect resistance. Its fine texture and good shade tolerance make it a popular component of shaded and low-input lawn seed mixes from the transition zone northward, either seeded alone or blended with other fine fescues or cool-season turf species. Sow in early fall into well-prepared, well-drained soil, keep consistently moist through germination, and expect reduced density in the deepest, most extreme shade.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Turfgrass Program

common_name: Beacon Hard Fescue (High-Vigor NTEP Top-Rated Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4–5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in lean, well-drained soil; Beacon establishes unusually quickly for a hard fescue thanks to high seedling vigor.

directions: Beacon is a hard fescue turf cultivar bred for improved durability, persistence, and visual quality under demanding, low-input growing conditions, and it has topped National Turfgrass Evaluation Program ratings for turf quality, density, seedling vigor, and red thread resistance among hard fescue entries. Its high seedling vigor lets it establish a dense stand more quickly than many older hard fescue cultivars, which is useful both for traditional low-mow lawns and for unmowed 'no-mow' meadow-style plantings. Like other hard fescues it tolerates poor, infertile, and acidic soils, needs little supplemental fertilizer, and handles dry shade better than Kentucky bluegrass or bermudagrass. Sow in early fall into lean, well-drained soil, and taper off irrigation once the stand is rooted in to keep growth appropriately slow and tough.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Turfgrass Seed Production

common_name: Seabreeze Creeping Red Fescue (Slender Cold- and Shade-Tolerant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4–5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall; Seabreeze is a slender creeping red fescue bred from a cross of slender creeping red and Chewings fescue, noted for winter color retention.

directions: Seabreeze is a slender creeping red fescue cultivar bred from a cross between slender creeping red fescue and Chewings fescue, released for its low, spreading growth habit and unusually good winter color, cold tolerance, and shade tolerance. Its fine texture and spreading rhizomes suit it to a wide range of uses, from cool-season putting green surrounds to open, unmowed golf course roughs and shaded slopes left natural. It performs well in shaded lawn areas where coarser turf species thin out, and it is often blended with Chewings and hard fescue in low-input, shade-tolerant lawn seed mixes. Sow in early fall into well-drained soil, keep evenly moist through germination, and expect the best shade performance in filtered rather than deep, dense shade.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Turfgrass Program
